children: By Adam Levine and Nate Wolf
Shares of Qualcomm fell sharply Wednesday after the chip maker reported better-than-expected revenue but warned of weaker margins ahead in its chip-design segment.

The results were a blow to Qualcomm shareholders, who began Wednesday celebrating a big new deal with SpaceX. Qualcomm will supply Elon Musk's rocket company with its Dragonwing cellular infrastructure platform.
The stock was down 5.9% in after-hours trading, erasing its 5.3% gain during regular trading.

Qualcomm reported adjusted earnings of $2.17 a share for the quarter, in line with Wall Street's consensus estimate of $2.16, per FactSet. Revenue fell 7% year over year to $10.4 billion, better than the $10.1 billion analysts had feared.

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, the company expects adjusted earnings of $2.25 a share, plus or minus 10 cents, on revenue between $10.4 billion and $11.2 billion. That guidance accounts for a 20% to 22% operating margin, excluding interest, in Qualcomm's chip-design segment, down from a 24% margin in the fourth quarter. Supply costs are to blame.
"The semiconductor industry is experiencing a broad-based increase in input costs across wafer fabrication, assembly, test, advanced packaging, memory and other materials," the company said.
This is breaking news. Read a preview of Qualcomm's earnings below and check back for more analysis soon.
Chip maker Qualcomm will report its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings Wednesday afternoon amid a slowdown in its core business and souring tech sentiment on Wall Street.

Qualcomm is synonymous with smartphone chips, but that market is getting crushed by high component prices, especially memory and storage chips, which are experiencing a generational shortage. According to Counterpoint Research, global smartphone unit shipments declined by 19% from the year before in the third quarter. Overall, Android phones were particularly hard hit, and Apple gained market share.

Apple has long used Qualcomm modem chips for cellular communications, but it has been substituting its own chips over time. Substantially fewer than 20% of Apple's new phones have Qualcomm modem chips in them anymore. Apple wants to replace all Qualcomm modems. Though it has taken years since it bought Intel's modem-chip unit in 2019 for $1 billion to jump-start the project, it is near completion.

Wall Street analysts expect fourth-quarter chip sales to be down 11% from last year to $8.7 billion, led by smartphone chip revenue declining by 25% to $5.2 billion, a result of Apple's moves and the mess in the Android market.
The stock is also getting caught up in the negative tech sentiment that has been seeping into markets. Qualcomm shares have fallen 11.3% over the past three trading days amid a broader tech selloff.

CEO Cristiano Amon put the company on a path to diversification years ago with chips for PCs, internet-of-things (IoT) devices and cars. Automotive chips have been the biggest individual success, with revenue projected at $1.7 billion, nearly a fifth of chip sales, up 60% from last year. Together, IoT and PC chip sales are seen down slightly to $1.8 billion. But the more diversified offerings are not large enough yet to offset this kind of weakness in Qualcomm's smartphone business.

The wild card is Qualcomm's nascent data center business, its biggest push outside consumer chips. The company has chips that run artificial-intelligence models. It has data center CPUs aimed at AI agents — software that can use AI models to accomplish complex series of tasks from simple conversational commands. Through the acquisition of Alphawave Semi last year, the company has networking chips and a business that designs custom chips for partners like Amazon.com.
A big customer is Humain, an AI company owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

Starting from practically nothing, Qualcomm is projecting $5 billion in data center revenue in fiscal year 2027, which just began, rising to more than $15 billion in fiscal 2029. In all, Qualcomm has issued guidance for $40 billion in non-phone sales that year, which would likely be substantially more than smartphone sales. Excluding Apple, Qualcomm expects smartphone chip sales to grow at around 5% a year.
But Qualcomm has also warned that its custom chips will have a lower gross profit margin than the rest of the company.
